Myth: an RTK drone means you no longer need ground control.

RTK improves the position of every photo. That is a real step forward. But independent check points, measured on the ground and not used in processing, are how you prove the final map is accurate.

Hiring a survey supplier? Ask for their check point report.

From flight to finished map in 20 seconds.

A photogrammetry survey has three stages: plan the area, fly parallel lines with enough overlap between photos, then process. The software matches features across overlapping photos to work out the shape of the ground, and produces an orthomosaic you can measure on and an elevation model.

Most of the quality is decided before take-off: flight height (which sets the ground sampling distance), overlap, and ground control.

posts.alt: RTK drones still need independent check points. Illustration of three checkerboard ground targets and a GNSS rover on site.
posts.text:
Myth vs fact: RTK drones and ground control.

RTK and PPK improve the position of every photo the drone takes, and that is a real advance for survey work.

But the number that matters to a client is the absolute accuracy of the final map, and the honest way to show it is independent check points: targets surveyed on the ground and kept out of processing. The difference between where the map puts them and where they really are is your accuracy.

When you hire a survey supplier, ask for the check point report. If there isn't one, ask why.

Myth: thermal cameras can see through walls.

They show differences in surface temperature, so people and vehicles stand out at night. But walls, roofs and glass block the view, and rain, fog and high humidity reduce how far a thermal camera can see clearly.

posts.text:
Orthomosaic, DSM, DTM: which one do you actually need?

Orthomosaic: a scale-correct map image. Measure distances and areas on it.
DSM (digital surface model): the height of everything on top, including trees, buildings and vehicles.
DTM (digital terrain model): the bare ground, with those removed. Contours are usually drawn from it.

Start from the question you need answered, then pick the output.

Faulty solar panels can look perfectly normal to the eye. A thermal drone flight shows what you miss.

A hot spot can point to damaged cells, a failed bypass diode or heavy soiling. It tells you where to look, not which fault it is.

Conditions matter: guidance for thermal inspection of PV plants (IEC TS 62446-3) calls for strong, stable sunlight of at least 600 W/m².

The drone finds and maps each anomaly; a technician confirms the cause on the ground.

Solar site to inspect? Request a pilot at aersynk.io.

posts.alt: Thermal inspection only works in the right conditions: a sun with 600 W/m2 or more, above a row of solar panels.
posts.text:
Solar PV thermography only works in the right conditions.

IEC TS 62446-3, the technical specification for thermographic inspection of PV plants, calls for strong, stable irradiance of at least 600 W/m² in the plane of the modules. Below that, the temperature differences that reveal faulty cells, failed bypass diodes and soiling may be too small to show reliably.

So a drone thermal inspection is planned around the weather and the time of day, not just the calendar. And a thermal anomaly is a pointer for a technician to confirm, not a diagnosis.

Planning a PV inspection? Request a pilot at https://aersynk.io

Stockpile volumes you can compare month to month.

A drone survey measures the whole surface of each pile as a dense 3D model, not a handful of spot heights. The volume is the space between that surface and a defined base.

Two things decide whether the monthly trend means anything: the base definition, stated in every report, and keeping the method and flight setup the same each month.

Need monthly volume surveys? Talk to us at https://aersynk.io

(Animated illustration, computer-generated voice.)

#StockpileManagement #Mining #DroneSurvey #Surveying #SouthAfrica

How does a drone measure a stockpile?

1. Overlapping photos become a dense 3D model of the whole surface.
2. Define the base the pile sits on, and state it in the report.
3. The volume is the space between the surface and the base.

Use the same method every month, and the trend actually means something.

Need monthly volume surveys? Send us a message or visit aersynk.io.

posts.alt: In-house drone team or hire a pilot? Two columns comparing when each makes sense.
posts.text:
In-house drone team, or hire a pilot?

In-house usually makes sense when flights are frequent and routine, and you have people to run the programme.

Hiring usually makes sense when flights are occasional, or need specialist sensors you would rarely use.

Either way, count the full cost of in-house: training, licensing, insurance, software, maintenance, and the time your team spends on it. The aircraft is usually the smallest part.

Working this out for your organisation? Ask about consulting at https://aersynk.io

#DroneProgramme #Drones #Operations #Mining #SouthAfrica

What does a drone dock actually do?

It is a weatherproof box that houses the drone, charges it and launches it. Missions can run on a schedule, like a daily site check, or on demand, and the data uploads to a cloud platform.

What it does not do: remove the rules. Remote operations still need an approved operator and a responsible remote pilot.

Thinking about docks for your site? Ask about consulting at aersynk.io.
